ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

Yubo Wang Affiliation: University of Waterloo Affiliation: Google    Rui Meng Affiliation: Google    Jaehyun Nam Affiliation: Google    Tomas Pfister Affiliation: Google    Jinsung Yoon Affiliation: Google
Abstract

Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost. 11 1 Project page: https://wyyyb.github.io/reprobridge_website/

1 Introduction

Reproducing a machine learning experiment often requires recovering details that its paper and released code leave implicit. A reproducer may resolve incompatible dependencies, identify the intended configuration, repair a data loader, and work out how run outputs become a reported score. Even a successful attempt can leave these decisions buried in conversations or shell histories, forcing the next reproducer to repeat the investigation. Code release is an essential starting point (Pineau et al., 2021); preserving the procedure recovered during execution is a further step toward reusable research artifacts (Stodden et al., 2016).

Coding-agent benchmarks expose this reconstruction burden through unresolved dependencies and misidentified outputs (Siegel et al., 2024), missing implementation details (Xiang et al., 2025), and plans that never become completed experiments (Starace et al., 2025). Consulting cited papers can recover some missing details (Zhao et al., 2026b), but successful execution may still depend on knowledge a capable agent supplies implicitly. How much does reproduction success depend on released artifacts, and how much on the reproducer’s ability to compensate for missing details?

Here, reproduction means independently re-executing machine-learning experiments using author-released materials, targeting numerically compatible measurements. Research artifacts comprise the code, data, checkpoints, environment specifications, and documentation supporting a study. Our hypothesis is that preserving the procedures and decisions recovered during reproduction can improve computational reproducibility. Dependency resolution can become an installation procedure; experiment discovery, a dedicated launcher; and a correction, a documented choice with its justification and affected tasks. We study this hypothesis through three contributions.

Artifact design.

We standardize a refined reproducible artifact with four components: a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide (Figure ; Section 3.2). Together they preserve executable procedures and the reasons for their settings and repairs. Component removals test the contribution of each part, while an ordinary-outputs control tests reuse of code, scripts, and logs without the standardized handoff.

Construction workflow.

ReproBridge constructs these artifacts from a paper and its official repository (Section 3.1). Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents specify experiments, prepare and execute them, and preserve the resulting procedures through review and packaging. Subsequent reuse is evaluated in fresh Reproducer sessions that receive either the raw codebase or the refined artifact.

Benchmark and empirical evaluation.

ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, with five human-verified reference scores per task (Section 2). Numerical compatibility is assessed against observed executions and their variability; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence because matching numbers alone can conceal substituted measurements. Across four coding agents, refined artifacts improve success by 5.5 to 23.2 pp and reduce downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%. Robustness analyses, component ablations, case studies, and human validation of the integrity checks examine the scope and mechanisms of these gains (Section 4).

2 Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench

2.1 Execution deviations and reference variation

A task specifies the data, model configuration, training or evaluation procedure, and reporting statistic to reproduce. The paper’s stated setup takes precedence over conflicting code. Let μ\mu be the expected value of that statistic when the specified experiment is faithfully executed. The published score is one observation, not an error-free value of μ\mu.

For an attempt producing a measurement YY, we write

Y=μ+D+ε.Y=\mu+D+\varepsilon.

Here DD is the shift in expectation from execution choices departing from the specified experiment, and ε\varepsilon is zero-mean variation conditional on them. This working model draws on the distinction between systematic and random effects in measurement (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2020; Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994). Stochastic training can vary between runs (Nagarajan et al., 2018). Independent repetitions can reduce uncertainty about the mean of a fixed procedure (Bouthillier et al., 2021), but do not remove a persistent shift DD. ReproBridge aims to reduce |D||D| by preserving procedures and decisions for faithful execution, while ε\varepsilon remains.

We use five human-verified reference observations of the same statistic per task. Assuming faithful and independent reference executions (D=0D=0), their mean estimates μ\mu, and their spread characterizes ε\varepsilon. A prediction interval accommodates uncertainty in that estimated center and variation in a new observation YY (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). Section 2.3 describes collection and verification. Numerical compatibility is combined with the execution-integrity checks in Section 4.1: a nearby number alone does not show that the intended experiment was performed.

2.2 Selection and units of analysis

The collection targets main experimental results with accessible official implementations. The sampling manifest starts with 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, identifies 241 with code and non-purely-theoretical content, and randomly samples 50. Excluding six for artifact or code availability, four for compute requirements, and four for closed-model access yields 36 retained test papers. Figure 1 summarizes their research areas and paired reproduction gains. ReproBridge and evaluation workflows were developed on ten papers, five from NeurIPS 2026 and five from ICLR 2026, scored under the same task, reference, and audit conventions and reported separately in Appendix D.7.

A task is one own-method measurement in a main table, identified by dataset, metric, reporting statistic, and location; selected main-table variants are retained. Baselines, stand-alone ablations, figures, and appendix-only results are excluded. An experiment can emit several task scores. The 36 papers yield 1,463 curated tasks from 502 experiments. Table 1 reports the full verification distribution: 1,029 tasks (70.3%) have numerically compatible reference results and form the downstream evaluation set, spanning 387 experiments. The remaining 434 tasks distinguish numerical disagreement from execution and resource barriers.

2.3 Reference collection and task verification

The reference protocol specifies five human reproducers on separate servers, starting from the same pinned raw commit with separate execution directories and coding-agent sessions. They must not reuse another participant’s generated scripts or measurements, refined artifacts, or downstream reproduction traces. Coding-agent assistance is permitted, but humans inspect the scripts, configurations, edits, and measurement extraction actually used. Before aggregation, the five reproducers’ execution setups were cross-verified against the paper’s specified setup and the common task definition. Each reference observation measures the specified task statistic: a multi-seed mean or best-of-NN statistic is one observation, not interchangeable with single-seed scores.

Verifiers must fix unspecified repetition and seed choices before inspecting scores, and must not tune procedures or repeat valid measurements until they approach the published value. Diagnostic runs and corrected reruns are recorded separately with reasons for replacement; numerical disagreement alone does not justify discarding a valid execution. Appendix A.3 gives the complete verification and evidence-retention protocol.

Numerical compatibility.

Following Section 2.1, the five observations estimate μ\mu and reference variation ε\varepsilon. For task jj, let pjp_{j} be the published score and xj​1,…,xj​5x_{j1},\ldots,x_{j5} the reference observations, with sample mean x¯j\bar{x}_{j} and sample standard deviation sjs_{j}. A reported range is represented by its midpoint. The compatibility interval is

Ij(q)=[x¯j−rj(q),x¯j+rj(q)],rj(q)=max⁡{t(1+q)/2,4​sj​1+15, 0.01​|x¯j|}.I_{j}^{(q)}=[\bar{x}_{j}-r_{j}^{(q)},\bar{x}_{j}+r_{j}^{(q)}],\qquad r_{j}^{(q)}=\max\left\{t_{(1+q)/2,4}s_{j}\sqrt{1+\tfrac{1}{5}},\;0.01|\bar{x}_{j}|\right\}. (1)

The default is q=0.95q=0.95. Without the explicit 1% tolerance floor, this is a Student-tt prediction interval for a new observation of the same statistic under an independent, approximately normal working model (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). It accommodates both uncertainty in the reference mean and variation in the new observation. Thresholds are fixed across raw and refined-artifact conditions; q=0.80q=0.80 supplies the stricter scoring check in Section 4.3.

Reference variability and task eligibility.

Categories 1 and 2 both require pj∈Ij(.95)p_{j}\in I_{j}^{(.95)}, and differ only in relative reference variability. We define

Vj=100​maxi⁡xj​i−mini⁡xj​i|pj|(pj≠0);Vj=+∞(pj=0).V_{j}=100\,\frac{\max_{i}x_{ji}-\min_{i}x_{ji}}{|p_{j}|}\quad(p_{j}\neq 0);\qquad V_{j}=+\infty\quad(p_{j}=0). (2)

Stable tasks satisfy Vj≤10V_{j}\leq 10, meaning that the reference range is at most 10% of the absolute published score; higher-variability tasks exceed this threshold. Both categories enter the downstream evaluation. We pool them for the main comparison and examine them separately in Section 4.3. Appendix A.4 gives the uncertainty derivation and additional details of the numerical rules.

2.4 Scope and information access

The evaluated set contains 631 full-procedure and 398 evaluation-only tasks (730 GPU, 299 CPU-only). Evaluating an explicitly permitted official checkpoint does not require repeating its training. Evaluation alone cannot establish completion of a training task.

All eight downstream conditions use the same task categories and numerical thresholds, applied outside the Reproducer session. Published targets remain visible in the paper and task specification; the Auditor checks that submitted values come from new executions. Session instructions withhold the reference information, alternative repository condition, and other agents’ run directories. An allowed checkpoint may serve as input; a shipped score file never counts as a measurement.

The benchmark includes 586 lower-is-better and 443 higher-is-better measurements, all assessed by the same two-sided compatibility rule. This evaluates agreement with the specified experimental result: a score beyond either bound remains numerically incompatible, including one that improves on the published value. Reference submissions must also link each score to the starting code commit, executed scripts and edits, environment and hardware, configuration and seeds, raw outputs, and score-extraction or aggregation procedure, making the reported statistic traceable to a concrete execution. Appendix A gives selection records, verification protocols, and statistical rules.

3 ReproBridge: artifact design and construction

ReproBridge turns reproduction work into an artifact that a later researcher or agent can use without access to the construction conversation. The handoff comprises refined code, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. Its construction workflow preserves the evidence behind execution choices as well as the executable steps themselves.

3.1 Construction workflow

Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents perform all construction, review, and packaging. Figure 2 organizes this work into three stages: Specify fixes the intended experiment before execution; Execute establishes a working procedure and records measurements, repairs, and failures; and Preserve packages that procedure and its rationale for reuse. Table 2 specifies each role’s inputs and persistent outputs.

Persistent evidence connects the stages.

A phase controller sequences the roles and checks required outputs between stages. Before scored execution, task specifications record the data, model, procedure, reporting statistic, source references, and unresolved choices. This makes execution decisions explicit before their results are known. When paper and code conflict, agents follow the paper’s setup and flag the discrepancy (Section 6). Each measurement must link to an actual output file; blocked tasks retain an explicit failure reason, and diagnostic runs remain separate from scored repetitions. The guide and change record are then grounded in these stored specifications, execution records, and justified repairs.

Independent review tests the evidence and the handoff.

A Reviewer inspects plans, execution records, and the completed artifact in contexts separate from the roles being reviewed. It returns localized findings to the responsible stage for revision and rechecking. Delivery also requires testing the supplied entry points from a clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition and checks on output structure and score extraction. The delivered environment must match the one used for construction measurements. Human reference information is withheld throughout construction. Appendix B gives the full role specifications and delivery checks.

3.2 Four components preserve execution knowledge

A later reproducer needs to know what code to run, how to prepare its environment, how to obtain the requested measurement, and why particular choices were made. The four-component refined reproducible artifact (RRA in figures and tables) addresses these needs. The refined codebase repairs execution defects and supplies missing experiment support. Environment setup specifies compatible dependencies and data or checkpoint acquisition. Experiment launchers connect tasks to configurations, execution scope, outputs, and measurement extraction, distinguishing scored runs from smoke tests. The reproduction guide, including its change record, explains settings, paper–code discrepancies, reporting statistics, and resource or numerical sensitivities. Section 4.5 tests the contribution of each component through removal experiments.

The guide connects instructions to their rationale. Each ambiguity entry records its source location, the gap, the adopted resolution and rationale, sensitivity, and affected tasks. The change record distinguishes execution fixes, correctness fixes, and convenience changes, while retaining pitfalls and open choices. Repetition guidance preserves the specified reporting unit and characterizes variation ε\varepsilon without selecting favorable outcomes. Figure 3 illustrates how SCIQL’s guide links measurement decisions and failure checks to executable support; Appendix B.2 expands its twelve-section structure.

4 Experiments

4.1 Evaluation protocol and setup

Opus 5 constructs the refined artifacts for the main experiment. Fresh Reproducer sessions receive the paper, selected tasks, and either raw code or its refined artifact. Construction conversations, hidden reference observations, and the alternative condition are withheld. Sessions submit new measurements and execution evidence; we compare success, token usage, and API spending.

Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Gemini 3.8 in figures and tables) attempt all 1,029 tasks from 36 test papers, with one fresh session per paper–model–condition per evaluation. Both raw-code and refined-artifact conditions use a 24-hour wall-clock limit per paper. GPU experiments use eight H100-80GB GPUs. Codex is the primary Auditor. Harnesses differ across vendors, so cross-model comparisons are descriptive. Paper-wise, stratified, and task-level diagnostics use the first evaluation. Appendix C details the harness, information boundaries, and auditing.

Execution-integrity audit.

An independent Auditor checks the evidence chain for each reported result, tracing the value to its output location, execution record, and generating script. It uses ledger timestamps to check execution and extraction order, and available script and output hashes to verify that the inspected files match the recorded versions. The Auditor cross-checks executed code, logs, and extracted values to locate copied measurements, altered outputs, or substituted computations.

After mechanical screening identifies leads, a Finder inspects executed code and records and proposes localized violations. A separate Refuter tries to overturn each proposed invalidation by checking the evidence, its effect on the measurement, and the task specification. Unsubstantiated findings remain uncertain. If the evidence remains contested, a panel examines its support, the measurement effect, and alternative explanations. The Auditor operates after reproduction and provides no feedback to the Reproducer.

Invalidation criteria and task success.

The five eligible violation classes distinguish copying a value without measuring it, substituting the measurement instrument, altering an operand used by the intended formula, choosing the reported outcome conditional on observed values, and computing the wrong statistic. Invalidation requires an eligible violation supported by localized evidence, a material effect on the measurement, and a failed refutation. A numerical mismatch, crashed run, hardware difference, or suspicion without a localized artifact does not automatically meet these conditions. Paper–code discrepancies are assessed against the same criteria.

A task succeeds when its result lies in the fixed compatibility interval (Equation 1) and is not invalidated by the primary Auditor; missing or incompatible results fail. Uncertain audit findings do not count as invalidations. Section 4.6 checks the sensitivity of this scoring rule to the Auditor and validates audit judgments against human review.

4.2 Refined artifacts improve success and reduce downstream cost

Refined artifacts improve success and lower downstream cost for every tested model (Table 3). Gains range from 5.5 pp for Opus 5, the strongest raw reproducer, to 23.2 pp for Gemini, with 6.3% to 19.8% fewer tokens and 16.8% to 23.7% lower API spending, including failed attempts. Cross-model summaries weight models equally; API savings are relative to each model’s raw-code cost.

The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 pp. This suggests that, given sufficient execution information, Reproducers with lower raw-code success can achieve high success. This supports our hypothesis that preserving execution knowledge reduces the need to infer missing details. Section 4.3 examines paper-level heterogeneity and scoring sensitivity.

External benchmark.

We compare handoffs on 45 CORE-Bench Hard capsules (Siegel et al., 2024); Sonnet 5 constructs the refined artifacts and VERITAS’s patched codebase and fix log (Liu et al., 2026a) (Table 4). Refined artifacts achieve the highest success, reduce median duration from 33 to 14 minutes, and lower spending per successful capsule from $8.43 to $4.34. VERITAS lies between raw and refined handoffs; the latter matches or exceeds raw success in each area.

4.3 Gains persist across papers and scoring thresholds

The main comparison pools task outcomes, so papers with more selected measurements contribute more weight. We examine whether gains persist when papers receive equal weight, when numerical scoring is stricter, and within each reference-variability group. These diagnostics use the first evaluation; Table 3 reports means over three evaluations.

Paper-level heterogeneity.

Figure 4 compares raw and refined-artifact success within each of the 36 papers. Paper-macro rates average these per-paper percentages with equal weight. All four models improve under this aggregation, with gains of 6.7 to 20.7 pp (Table 5a). Success improves or ties on 30 to 33 papers per model, while three to six papers regress. Thus the aggregate gains extend across papers, although refinement does not improve every paper. Section 4.4 examines remaining failures and task-level reversals.

Stricter numerical compatibility.

Replacing the default 95% interval with the 80% interval in Equation 1 preserves the selected tasks and the primary Auditor’s judgments. Refined artifacts still improve success for every model, with gains of 10.3 to 39.1 pp (Table 5b). The positive gains therefore persist under a tighter numerical criterion.

Reference variability.

Both reference-variability groups improve across all four models, with larger point-estimate gains in Cat. 1: 8.0 to 23.3 pp versus 2.1 to 22.3 pp in Cat. 2. The groups differ in task composition and interval width, so this contrast is descriptive. Appendix D provides the full stratified results.

4.4 Preserved procedures support recovery and reduce reconstruction

Case studies and qualitative analyses use the first evaluation. Across paired task–model outcomes, 813 raw failures become successes, against 136 reversals (Figure 5). Recoveries include 348 numerical mismatches, 210 unexecuted tasks due to execution or resource barriers (Not run), and 255 audit-invalid numerical matches. These records suggest two complementary contributions: completing ambiguous or incomplete measurement specifications and preserving executable procedures for reuse.

Completing and clarifying measurement specifications.

In Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts (De Santis et al., 2026), the reduction of multiple tree-edit distances is unspecified, and the released code lacks a collector for Table 1. Sonnet 5’s raw attempt sums the four distances, reporting 60 rather than 15. The refined artifact resolves this ambiguity by specifying the per-expression mean and supplying the collector; the later attempt reports 15. SCIQL’s released code similarly leaves the mapping from run outputs to table entries incomplete; the refined artifact specifies the output field and aggregation across criteria and seeds. Such clarification and experiment-to-result mapping together represent about 35% of the case-review attribution distribution.

Recovered configurations become executable: HELIX.

For HELIX (Zhang et al., 2026a), Opus 5 restores the paper’s architecture on raw code but retains the shipped batch size and learning rate. The refined artifact identifies a repository revision matching that architecture, records it as the source of the adopted settings, and exposes them through a launcher. A later attempt produces numerically compatible MAEs for both illustrated tasks. The guide records the evidence for the choice, and the launcher makes it reusable (Appendix D.5).

A compatible environment transfers across sessions: WBMM.

For six COCO tasks in WBMM (Song et al., 2026), Sonnet 4.6’s raw attempt fails to install a compatible vision-library stack for H100. The refined artifact preserves the dependency versions, build prerequisite, and source-build route for the target architecture. The later session executes all six tasks without a code patch; its box and mask AP values agree numerically with the reported targets. This case shows how an environment repair can become a reusable installation procedure (Appendix D.5).

Fixing bugs in the released code.

In Effective Model Pruning (Wang et al., 2026), the released loader silently labels all 10,000 TinyImageNet validation images as one class. During construction, ReproBridge adds a script organizing images by their true labels and a launcher check requiring prepared data. In paired Gemini 3.8 Flash runs, ResNet-18 validation loss changes from 8.898 on raw code to 2.288 with the refined artifact, close to the paper’s 2.303. Model–paper sessions changing code downstream fall from 113/144 to 54/144, and median time to first scored execution decreases for every model (Figure 5, right). Together with lower token use, this indicates less reconstruction.

Explicit procedures also help the model that built them.

Clearer code organization and explicit execution decisions can reduce repeated search and context demands, even for the model that built the artifact. In ETTFS (Che et al., 2026), the raw Opus 5 attempt searches 6,377 lines of Python for measurement code absent from the release. The refined artifact organizes the added measurement code into a dedicated profiling module, a launcher that sequences training and profiling, and documented output fields. A fresh Opus 5 session follows this structure and completes a previously blocked measurement.

Remaining failures.

Failures shared by both handoffs mainly reflect paper–code setup mismatches, typographical errors in the paper, or experimental variability placing measurements outside the compatibility interval. Refinement can also preserve or introduce incorrect experimental choices.

The 136 reversals from raw success to refined failure comprise 84 numerical mismatches, 31 resource/access failures, 11 audit-invalid matches, and 10 execution blockers. AuxiliaryMCMC and LiME account for 50 and 14 reversals, respectively, or 47.1% combined. The LiME case (Kowsher et al., 2026) illustrates an attempt that fails to complete training and evaluation; AuxiliaryMCMC (Yuan and Wang, 2026) illustrates numerical fragility, hardware sensitivity, and protocol deviations under time pressure (Appendix D.3).

4.5 Each artifact component contributes to reuse

Ordinary outputs are Opus 5’s raw-code execution directory with code, scripts, and logs retained and result files removed. They carry no standardized guide.

Component-removal protocol.

Refined-code removal restores the original source; environment removal deletes the setup route; launcher removal deletes the experiment entry points. For these three conditions, descriptions of the removed component are also deleted from the remaining documentation and scripts. The guide ablation removes the guide itself. The change record belongs to the documentation component.

A source file and an explanation of how to reconstruct it can carry overlapping knowledge. Deleting only the file leaves a route for the downstream agent to restore the same functionality. Removing both the component and its descriptions tests the loss of that information while leaving the other components available; the resulting losses are conditional on those retained materials.

The full artifact improves on ordinary outputs.

The complete artifact outperforms ordinary outputs by 11.8 pp (Table 6). Ordinary outputs also outperform raw code, demonstrating value in reusing execution work. Both handoffs come from separate upstream runs with comparable resource use. The comparison evaluates protocol-guided construction and its resulting handoff.

Code and environment removal cause the largest losses, showing the need for repaired implementations and compatible dependencies. Removing the guide or launchers also reduces success when code and environment remain available: an executable codebase can still leave settings, measurement rules, and entry points implicit. Retained components can partly compensate for a removal (Appendix D.4). These losses favor pairing executable support with explicit guidance on measuring results.

4.6 Gains persist across Auditors despite imperfect detection

Sensitivity to the Auditor.

Codex and Claude inspect the same numerically matching outcomes in the first evaluation (Table 7). Refined artifacts improve success under either Auditor for every model. Differences in invalidations change the absolute success rates, while the direction of the raw-to-refined comparison is preserved.

Validation against human review.

Two human reviewers cross-verified all 409 selected tasks from eight randomly selected papers under both Raw and RRA conditions, totaling 818 outcomes. Review includes outcomes not flagged by either Auditor. Each reviewer traces the measurement to primary execution evidence, records an initial judgment, and cross-checks the other’s assessment before they agree on the final label. Selection is at the paper level, and task outcomes can share execution evidence. Appendix C.4 gives the complete protocol.

Against the shared human labels (Figure 6), Codex achieves 88.6% precision and 79.5% recall, versus Claude’s 85.7% and 61.5%. Each Auditor falsely flags four of 779 valid outcomes (0.5%). Codex detects seven more invalid outcomes at the same false-positive count. The shared labels identify 39 invalid outcomes: 33 with Raw and six with RRA. Codex misses eight of these outcomes, and Claude misses 15.

In a WBMM timing case, reports replace measured epoch durations with full-dataset projections, including 32.5 seconds reported as 206 seconds; files are edited after process exit. These projections do not constitute the requested measurements. The measured durations also satisfy the numerical intervals, making execution evidence decisive for detecting the substitution. Before invalidation, the Refuter checks the measurement effect and whether permitted protocol choices explain the apparent violation. Appendix C presents the human-review protocol and additional audit cases.

4.7 Repeated reuse can offset construction API cost

Constructing the 36 artifacts costs $5,026 in API usage ($139.61 per paper). At the mean downstream costs in Table 3, break-even requires 8, 13, and 9 reuse rounds for Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, and Opus 5, respectively. Each round repeats all 36 papers; the scenario charges the full construction cost to one model, holds prices and savings fixed, and excludes GPU, auditing, and maintenance costs. The corresponding API savings are $653, $409, and $615 per complete reuse round, respectively. Higher success accompanies these savings, so reuse improves reproduction while progressively recovering the construction investment. Appendix E details the accounting rates and break-even calculation.

5 Related work

Scientific trust and computational reproducibility.

Scientific trust depends on collective scrutiny and accessible evidence (Oreskes, 2019; Nosek et al., 2015; Munafò et al., 2017); AI-assisted research retains these requirements (Messeri and Crockett, 2024). Following ACM terminology, reproducibility means independent execution of authors’ artifacts, rather than independent reimplementation or bitwise-identical replay (Association for Computing Machinery, 2020; Peng, 2011). Reproducibility Enhancement Principles and the NeurIPS reproducibility program promote explicit dependencies, code release, and reporting checklists (Stodden et al., 2016; Pineau et al., 2021).

Research reproduction benchmarks.

PaperBench assesses reconstruction through expert rubrics covering code, execution, and results (Starace et al., 2025); SciReplicate-Bench also studies implementation reconstruction (Xiang et al., 2025). REPRO-Bench and ReplicationBench extend assessment to social science and astrophysics (Hu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). CORE-Bench tests execution of released Code Ocean capsules and questions about their outputs (Siegel et al., 2024). ReproBridge-Bench evaluates released artifacts through binary task success, combining intervals based on variability across five human-verified executions with an independent integrity audit. Tasks include GPU training and evaluation. Table 4 compares handoffs under CORE-Bench’s scoring rule.

Automated reproduction and reusable experience.

PaperCoder constructs repositories through planning and code generation (Seo et al., 2026). AutoReproduce recovers implicit details from cited papers and evaluates execution fidelity (Zhao et al., 2026b). VERITAS executes research procedures and produces patched code, fix records, and claim assessments (Liu et al., 2026a); our external comparison tests reuse of its handoff. Reflexion retains verbal feedback, while Voyager accumulates executable skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). The Compiler for Agent-Native Research Artifacts (ARA) (Liu et al., 2026b) packages papers and repositories with expert rubrics in its PaperBench study; a model judge scores reproduction against those rubrics. We construct runnable four-component handoffs without evaluation rubrics or human reference scores, and assess their value through four component removals and an ordinary-outputs control.

6 Discussion and limitations

The four component contracts make reproduction experience reusable, and ReproBridge-Bench provides verified reference scores for evaluation. We study their roles together; the delivery protocol guides what ReproBridge recovers and preserves during construction. In the formulation of Section 2.1, the aim is to reduce avoidable deviations DD while documenting uncertainty about the intended experiment.

6.1 Use before submission and by later reproducers

The primary intended use is for authors to apply ReproBridge as a reproducibility check before submitting a paper and releasing its artifacts. Executing the paper’s specified setup can expose missing details, execution barriers, and paper–code inconsistencies, giving authors concrete issues to inspect and correct before submission. Third-party reproducers can likewise preserve their work in the same format to lower the cost of later attempts. A human reader can use the setup route and launchers to execute experiments, then inspect the guide and change record to assess the settings and repairs. Our experiments measure reuse by coding agents.

6.2 Paper–code misalignment

When the paper and released code conflict, ReproBridge strictly follows the paper’s setup and flags the discrepancy with source locations and affected tasks. For example, the Manifold-Aware Perturbations guide identifies a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} in the paper versus 10−310^{-3} in the released code. Such records help authors check consistency between their manuscript and implementation during the pre-submission review described above.

A separate agent-assisted static analysis records 238 in-scope contradiction findings touching 669 distinct selected tasks. A contradiction requires an explicit paper statement and conflicting implemented behavior; absent implementations and choices on which the paper is silent are recorded separately. These findings are possible sources of execution deviation DD, but their effects on measured performance require controlled comparisons. They are neither human-validated error rates nor explanations of the measured gains. The analysis is separate from primary success scoring, and its records were not supplied to evaluated Reproducers. Appendix D.6 documents the scope, categories, and evidence.

6.3 Limitations

The evaluation conditions on retained papers, fixed reference regions, and the tested agents; it is not a conference-wide reproduction rate. Five reference observations are a protocol choice, not a guarantee of adequate uncertainty estimation. Numerical compatibility does not certify scientific validity or complete fidelity to the stated experiment, and refined artifacts can preserve incorrect assumptions. Automated audits also miss some violations, as quantified against human verification.

The complete artifact intervention includes upstream investigation, repair, review, and packaging. Ordinary outputs and refined artifacts are produced in separate runs with comparable upstream resource use. This comparison evaluates the construction workflow and resulting handoff together; it does not isolate the effect of reorganizing identical outputs. Component ablations measure losses conditional on the remaining materials. Case annotations and variability strata describe patterns rather than isolate causal effects.

API savings concern downstream Reproducer sessions. Construction, independent verification, GPU execution, maintenance, and human review have separate costs; reuse estimates assume fixed prices and savings. Human time savings and comprehension require a separate study.

7 Conclusion

ReproBridge standardizes recovered reproduction procedures and decisions into four reusable components: a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. ReproBridge-Bench provides verified reference scores to assess their value. Reproduction success depends jointly on artifact quality and reproducer ability. All four evaluated models achieve mean reproduction success above 90% with refined artifacts, including those with lower raw-code success. The cross-model success-rate spread and downstream API spending both decrease. Removing code or environment setup causes the largest ablation losses; removing guides or launchers also reduces success with the other components retained.

Future work should evaluate reuse by human researchers and measure the full costs of constructing, verifying, and maintaining artifacts across repeated attempts.

AI use statement

Coding agents constructed the refined artifacts, performed downstream reproductions, and produced automated integrity audits as part of the experiments (Sections 3 and 4.1). They also assisted human reference reproducers with setup, debugging, and script preparation under human verification (Appendix A.3). Agent-assisted reviews annotated recovered outcomes and paper–code discrepancies; these annotations are descriptive and do not establish causal effects or human-validated error rates (Appendices D.2 and D.6).

We used generative AI to draft and edit text, write and check analysis scripts, and prepare figure designs that were redrawn as editable diagrams. The authors defined the research question, hypothesis, benchmark, workflow, and evaluation protocols; reviewed all AI-assisted work; and checked the reported numbers and statistical plots against the recorded results and frozen analysis inputs. We did not use generative AI to generate synthetic data. The authors take responsibility for the final text, claims, and artifacts.
