Appendix A Benchmark and reference protocol

This appendix covers selection, reference verification, statistical rules, and paper inventories.

A.1 Task selection and reporting units

Extraction and reporting units.

Each retained task has a paper identifier, task identifier, source experiment identifier, paper-table locator, reported score, metric direction, task type, and compute type. The selected set contains 730 GPU tasks and 299 CPU-only tasks; 586 have lower-is-better metrics and 443 higher-is-better metrics. Absolute interval membership is used in both cases: outperforming the target in one direction does not automatically satisfy numerical compatibility. Of the 36 papers, 28 are classified as GPU papers and eight as CPU-only papers.

Sampling and exclusions.

The supplied sampling manifest records 742 Spotlight papers, a mechanically filtered pool of 241 papers with code and non-purely-theoretical content, a random sample of 50, and 36 retained papers. Its primary exclusion categories are artifact/code availability (six), compute requirements (four), and closed-model dependence (four). The compute criteria concern papers for which more than half of the main experiments require over 100 H100 GPU-hours per experiment or more than one eight-H100 node; the API criterion concerns more than half of the main experiments. These are selection criteria, not measured universal execution budgets. Tables 9 and 10 provide the retained and excluded inventories.

A.2 Primary research-area assignments

Figure 1 uses eight topic families adapted from the ICML 2026 research topics, further divided into 22 subdomains.22 2 https://icml.cc/Conferences/2026/CallForPapers We merge general machine learning with theory, and machine learning systems with optimization; the other six directions remain separate. Each paper receives one editorial assignment by its primary contribution; these are not its original conference submission labels. Generative models fall under deep learning; interpretability, verification, safety, privacy, and causality fall under trustworthy ML. For cross-cutting work, tabular compression is assigned to systems and optimization, conditioned diffusion bridges to probabilistic methods, and brain modeling and survival-data generation to application-driven ML. Table 8 gives the complete primary-area mapping.

Development and test.

Five NeurIPS 2026 papers and five ICLR 2026 papers supported development of construction, reproduction, and audit workflows. They follow the same task extraction, reference, and integrity-check conventions as test papers. Their results are therefore comparable under the same scoring definition, but they are not held out from workflow development. Results and costs are reported separately in Table 3 for the 36-paper test set and Appendix D.7 for development.

A.3 Human reference-verification protocol

For reference collection, a human verifier is a participant responsible for both reproducing an experiment and checking its execution evidence. The following requirements apply to each of the five participants in Section 2.3; this role is distinct from human validation of the downstream Auditors.

Common starting point and independent execution.

Each verifier must use a separate server and a fresh checkout of the same pinned raw-repository commit, together with the paper, common task specification, and authorized supporting artifacts. Execution directories and coding-agent sessions must remain separate. Verifiers must not reuse another participant’s generated scripts or measurements, constructed refined artifacts, or downstream reproduction traces. Published scores remain visible in the paper but cannot substitute for newly computed measurements.

Experimental fidelity and documented repairs.

Before aggregating the reference measurements, the five verifiers’ executed scripts, configurations, and reporting procedures were cross-verified to confirm that the executions followed the paper’s specified setup and the common task definition. Verification must check the task’s dataset and split, preprocessing, model configuration, training procedure, and evaluation metric against that setup, including required hardware and numerical precision, and inspect the released implementation for consistency. A training task cannot be replaced by checkpoint evaluation; an official checkpoint is permitted when the task explicitly specifies evaluation-only reproduction. Necessary environment or implementation fixes must retain the intended experiment, with their rationale and differences from the starting commit recorded. Material ambiguities must be documented rather than resolved by selecting whichever interpretation best matches the published score.

Human responsibility for agent-assisted work.

Coding agents may assist with setup, debugging, and script preparation. The human verifier must inspect the scripts and configuration actually executed, including agent-generated edits, data loading, checkpoint selection, and metric extraction. Verification must connect the reported value to the computation that produced it, rather than rely on an agent’s summary, a successful exit code, or numerical proximity alone. A measurement whose execution fidelity cannot be established must not be accepted as a reference score.

Consistent reporting units and repetitions.

Each participant must produce one complete observation of the specified reporting statistic per task. For a multi-seed mean, this includes all required seed-level runs and their prescribed aggregation; for best-of-NN, it includes all NN candidates and the specified selection rule. Constituent runs must not be pooled across participants to create the five reference observations. Seed choices, repetition counts, and stopping rules must follow the task protocol; unspecified choices must be documented and fixed before inspecting the resulting scores. Prescribed fixed seeds do not remove the requirement for separate executions.

No score-driven selection or substitution.

Verifiers must not tune procedures or repeat valid measurements until they approach the paper’s score. Diagnostic runs and corrected reruns must be distinguished from reference measurements, with the reason for replacement recorded; numerical disagreement alone is not grounds for discarding a valid execution. Failed or resource-blocked attempts must retain their failure reason, without substituting cached scores, another participant’s result, or an imputed value. Numerical compatibility is assessed after execution verification using the common rules in Section 2.3.

Evidence retention and information separation.

Each submitted observation must identify its task, verifier, execution, starting commit, executed scripts and edits, environment and hardware, configuration and seeds, raw outputs, and score-extraction or aggregation procedure. The verification record must state what was checked and any unresolved deviations. Reference measurements and verification guidance must remain separate from ReproBridge and downstream Reproducer inputs. These requirements support execution fidelity; the statistical assumptions for combining the five observations are specified separately in Appendix A.4.

A.4 Error model and reference rules

We expand the formulation in Section 2.1 and give additional details of the compatibility and category rules defined in Section 2.3.

A.4.1 Execution error and reference uncertainty

Let πj\pi_{j} specify the intended data, configuration, execution conditions, and reporting statistic for task jj. Its target is μj=𝔼πj​[Yj]\mu_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{j}}[Y_{j}], the expected result under that procedure. A paper score pjp_{j} has realized discrepancy pj−μjp_{j}-\mu_{j}; neither its magnitude nor its cause is determined by the published value alone. If the reporting unit is a multi-seed mean or best-of-NN statistic, YjY_{j} denotes that entire statistic.

For attempts yielding a computed result, let ZZ denote the realized execution procedure, including choices reconstructed from the supplied information. Expectations describe repeated attempts for a fixed task, agent, and artifact condition. Suppressing these indices, define

m⁡(Z)=𝔼⁡[Y∣Z],D=m⁡(Z)−μ,ε=Y−m⁡(Z).m(Z)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z],\qquad D=m(Z)-\mu,\qquad\varepsilon=Y-m(Z). (A.1)

Then 𝔼⁡[ε∣Z]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid Z]=0 and 𝔼⁡[D​ε]=0\mathbb{E}[D\varepsilon]=0. With finite second moments, conditioning on the procedure gives

𝔼⁡[(Y−μ)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu)^{2}] =𝔼⁡[(m⁡(Z)−μ)2]+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Y∣Z)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(m(Z)-\mu)^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z)] (A.2)
=(𝔼​D)2+Var⁡(D)+𝔼⁡[ε2].\displaystyle=(\mathbb{E}D)^{2}+\operatorname{Var}(D)+\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{2}].

The first two terms capture persistent mean shifts and variation in those shifts across reconstructed procedures. The last captures variation conditional on the procedure. This distinction is analogous to between-condition and within-condition effects in measurement models (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2020). For a faithful fixed procedure, D=0D=0; conversely, D=0D=0 alone does not prove fidelity, since different procedures can have the same expected score. Nor must the residual variance be equal across raw and refined-artifact conditions. Independent repetitions of an unchanged procedure reduce the variance of its mean, not a persistent shift in its expected value.

What five reference observations estimate.

Under a faithful reference model, Xj​iX_{ji} are independent observations of the same reporting statistic under comparable execution conditions, with mean μj\mu_{j} and variance σj,ref2\sigma^{2}_{j,\mathrm{ref}}. Let X¯j\bar{X}_{j} be their sample mean and sjs_{j} the observed sample standard deviation. Thus 𝔼⁡[X¯j]=μj\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_{j}]=\mu_{j} and Var⁡(X¯j)=σj,ref2/5\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}_{j})=\sigma^{2}_{j,\mathrm{ref}}/5. Approximate normality motivates the Student-tt construction. A confidence interval for μj\mu_{j} has half-width t0.975,4​sj/5t_{0.975,4}s_{j}/\sqrt{5} (NIST/SEMATECH, n.d.); a prediction interval for a new observation instead has half-width t0.975,4​sj​1+1/5t_{0.975,4}s_{j}\sqrt{1+1/5} (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). The latter includes both reference-center uncertainty and the new observation’s variability. Equation 1 additionally imposes the explicit 1% tolerance floor.

If a downstream measurement YY is independent of these unbiased reference observations, then

𝔼⁡[(Y−X¯j)2]=𝔼⁡[(Y−μj)2]+σj,ref25.\mathbb{E}[(Y-\bar{X}_{j})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu_{j})^{2}]+\frac{\sigma^{2}_{j,\mathrm{ref}}}{5}. (A.3)

Squared distance to the reference mean therefore also contains reference-estimation uncertainty. The paper uses the decomposition to motivate knowledge preservation, not to report empirically identified bias or variance components.

A.4.2 Additional details of the numerical rules

Section 2.3 defines the compatibility interval (Equation 1) and reference-variation measure (Equation 2). The tt multipliers for q=0.95q=0.95 and q=0.80q=0.80 are approximately 2.78 and 1.53; calculations retain the stored precision. The 1% tolerance floor is active on 197 retained tasks. There is no additional near-zero rule for VjV_{j}: all 21 retained zero-target tasks belong to the higher-variability group. A compatibility interval can contain the reported score even when the five observations do not bracket it.

A.5 Retained and excluded paper inventories

Appendix B Artifact design and construction

This appendix expands the construction contracts in Section 3.1 and Table 2 with full role instructions and the artifact’s document structure.

B.1 Construction-skill specifications

ReproBridge implements artifact construction through role-specific skills, each with instructions, reference protocols, tools, and required outputs. The specifications below expand the construction contracts and coordination described in Section 3.1 and Table 2. Separate downstream Reproducer and Auditor workflows evaluate the artifacts; human reference collection and human audit validation belong to benchmark development and evaluation, respectively.

Intake.

Read the complete paper, including appendices, before planning. Preserve the selected task list and pinned raw commit. Map each task to its table entry, survey the implementation, check required artifacts, and record missing details. Do not silently substitute an unavailable repository revision or redefine a task to fit the available code.

Planner.

For each task, specify the measurement, data, procedure, aggregation, and stated repetitions, with references to supporting paper passages or code locations. Group tasks that share an execution. Record the adopted resolution of each ambiguity before the dependent run; prepare an executable plan and launcher. The Planner does not execute experiments. When paper and code conflict, strictly follow the paper’s stated setup, flag the conflicting code and affected tasks, and record the required implementation corrections before the dependent run.

Builder.

Resolve and record dependencies, provide reproducible acquisition of required data and checkpoints, and test the resulting environment. The environment described by the deliverable should be the one used for construction measurements, not an untested reconstruction assembled afterward. Environment work must not silently change the experimental plan.

Construction Reproducer.

Execute planned experiments in the prepared environment. Link values to actual output files and record commands, resources, and failures. Distinguish diagnostic runs from scored repetitions; justify changes and repetition extensions. Do not silently edit a frozen plan or select favorable repetitions in place of the specified reporting statistic. Every task needs a supported measurement or an explicit, evidenced reason why none was produced.

Distiller.

Write the guide and change record from stored task specifications, execution evidence, repairs, and choices. Explain the reporting statistic, observed variability, resource requirements, pitfalls, and uncovered scope. Preserve uncertainty where the record does not resolve it. Historical measurements belong in separate result records, not in instructions substituting for new measurements.

Packager.

Assemble the code, environment, launchers, and documentation actually used. Check portable paths and verify the handoff from a clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition. Compare the output structure and extraction route with the record. Do not invent replacement values or treat a successful smoke test as completion of a scientific experiment.

Reviewer.

Check the plan before scored execution, inspect evidence and recorded changes during reproduction, and test the final handoff as an unfamiliar user. Inspect the underlying files and outputs directly instead of accepting another role’s summary. Produce localized findings with the responsible role; do not repair and approve the same work in one context.

Alignment extension.

The Aligner skill extracts paper-side requirements before inspecting their implementation, then records contradictions separately from missing code and unspecified details. It does not execute experiments, edit plans, or infer a measured performance effect from a plausible mechanism. Appendix D.6 describes the separate analysis.

B.2 Four-component handoff and document structure

The normalized refined artifact has seven top-level entries:

Path Role
src/ Derived source code
Dockerfile Preferred container setup
setup/ Environment lock, installation, and data scripts
experiments/ Launchers and shared path setup
reproduction_guideline.md Reproduction guide
change_log.md Change record and open choices
verify.sh Package verification entry point

The archive additionally separates reproduction-result pages and paper–code alignment records. The manuscript’s “change record” refers to change_log.md.

The normalized guide has twelve sections: purpose, hardware, software, environment setup, artifacts, experiments, repetitions and variance, expected output structure, paths, ambiguities and unspecified details, pitfalls, and uncovered scope. Its environment section distinguishes Docker from installation scripts. The ambiguity table records ID, type, location, gap, adopted resolution and reason, sensitivity, and affected tasks. The change record uses six sections: changes required to run, changes required for correctness, convenience changes, deliberately unchanged behavior, pitfalls, and open choices.

Across the 36 packaged repositories, normalized documents contain 932 ambiguity-table entries. The corpus contains 482 launcher scripts, including those outside the retained scoring scope.

Figure 7 expands SCIQL’s twelve-section guide with representative instructions and decisions.

Appendix C Evaluation protocol and audit validation

The evaluation uses fresh downstream sessions and a separate integrity audit. The following settings, information boundaries, and validation protocol concern this evaluation, not artifact construction.

Test-set diagnostic statistics here and in Appendix D report a single evaluation; Table 3 and the cost summary in Table 21 use means over three evaluations.

C.1 Model configurations and information boundaries

Visibility.

Construction permits the paper, raw repository, required artifacts, and the agents’ own execution feedback, while excluding human reference guidance. Reproducers receive the paper and published targets, the selected task specification, and their assigned repository. Reference categories and hidden score fields are removed from session input; the external evaluator retains the exported thresholds. Instructions prohibit using other runs or the alternative repository and require submitted measurements to originate in the current run. Some guides describe historical result directions or magnitudes. The Auditor checks whether submitted measurements come from new executions.

Execution records.

The downstream Reproducer workflow stores execution IDs, output files and locators, task evidence, and code differences. Where recorded, script/file hashes and ordering checks provide additional provenance evidence. Resource accounting distinguishes wrapped-execution device-hours from total reserved-lane device-hours. Both raw-code and refined-artifact conditions use the same 24-hour wall-clock limit per paper. This session limit applies to downstream evaluation; the experiment-level compute criterion governs benchmark eligibility.

C.2 Independent reproduction skill

A fresh downstream Reproducer session uses the repro-run execution skill. It receives the assigned repository, paper, and selected tasks, then plans experiment scripts, prepares permitted inputs, schedules executions, extracts values, and reports code changes and evidence locators. The session retains responsibility for the final evidence, including work delegated by the harness.

Programmatic support freezes inputs, schedules work under the resource limits, links values to files, and checks evidence consistency. Scientific assessment combines these records with inspection of the paper and executed code.

C.3 Additional audit coordination

Section 4.1 defines the Finder–Refuter procedure and invalidation criteria; Table 7 compares the two Auditors on the same numerically matching outcomes. Codex supplies the primary success labels, while Claude supplies a sensitivity comparison. For either Auditor, success is the number of numerical matches minus invalidations, divided by 1,029 tasks.

Unresolved screening leads require recorded dispositions, and final task-level verdicts are assembled from structured findings. Separate sessions and withheld prior verdicts reduce direct self-validation and cross-auditor anchoring. The human verification protocol below assesses both Auditors against the same evidence requirements.

C.4 Two-person human verification protocol

Two human auditors cross-verified selected Reproducer outcomes. The protocol below defines this review’s evidence requirements and cross-checking responsibilities. It evaluates existing execution records; human reference collection (Appendix A.3) generates numerical reference observations.

Review scope and unit.

Both reviewers must examine each selected task–condition outcome, including outcomes not flagged by either automated Auditor. Reviewing only automated disagreements or invalid flags would miss violations accepted by both systems. Shared executions may support several judgments, but each alleged violation must be linked to the affected task scores; a problem in one experiment does not automatically invalidate every result in the paper.

Trace the measurement to primary evidence.

Each reviewer must connect the submitted score to the executed command, scripts and configuration, input artifacts, raw outputs, and extraction or aggregation procedure. The supplied code and subsequent changes must be inspected to establish the computation underlying the scored result. Review must also check for copied values, substituted measurements, result-dependent selection, incorrect reductions, and altered execution records. Automated explanations can identify claims to inspect, but are not evidence by themselves.

Apply the same invalidation criteria.

Reviewers must apply the invalidation criteria in Section 4.1, considering permitted reporting rules and environment or resource effects before confirming a violation. Judgments concern the executed procedure and its evidence rather than inferred intent.

Cross-check judgments and resolve disagreements.

Each reviewer must record a judgment and its supporting evidence before the pair compares assessments. Each must then check the other’s task mapping, supporting files and outputs, and interpretation, including counterevidence. Disagreements must be resolved by returning to the execution record and documenting why a judgment is retained or revised, not by treating either automated Auditor as a tie-breaker. Both reviewers must endorse the final human label and its rationale; an unresolved case must not be presented as an agreed judgment.

Retain the review record and compare verdicts.

The record must retain task and condition identifiers, the associated execution, both initial judgments, evidence locators, any disagreement and its resolution, and the final cross-verified label. Correctness of an automated verdict must be evaluated against this human label, separately from whether its explanation identifies the correct mechanism. Count each task–condition outcome once when computing detection statistics, even when several outcomes share execution evidence.

C.4.1 Human-verified subset

Eight papers are randomly selected from the test set for two-person cross-verification: ExactFANOVA (82 tasks), Learning Randomized Reductions (38), ATLAS (82), MindOmni (53), POET-X (57), SlaClip (30), Weak-and-Strong Verification (9), and WBMM (58). Review covers all 409 tasks from these papers in both conditions: 409 raw-codebase and 409 refined-artifact outcomes, totaling 818 task–condition outcomes. It identifies 39 invalid outcomes: 33 with raw code and six with refined artifacts. The remaining 779 outcomes are valid under this review, comprising 376 raw-codebase and 403 refined-artifact outcomes. Invalid is the positive class, and uncertain audit judgments are negative. Precision divides correct invalid detections by all invalid predictions; recall divides them by all human-confirmed invalid outcomes. Random selection occurs at the paper level; task outcomes within a paper can share execution evidence and should not be treated as independent draws.

Codex misses eight of 39 human-confirmed invalid outcomes (20.5%); Claude misses 15 (38.5%). Each incorrectly flags four of 779 human-verified valid outcomes (0.5%). Codex detects a larger fraction of invalid outcomes in each condition, while Claude makes no false positive on the refined artifact subset (Table 12).

C.5 Qualitative audit cases

These cases illustrate measurement validity and evidence integrity through execution records.

Timing reports versus executed measurements: WBMM.

For refined-artifact tasks T028, T033, and T038, execution records show epoch times of approximately 32.5, 53, and 92 seconds. Submitted JSON and local logs instead contain 206, 335, and 579 seconds, obtained by projecting subset timings to a 2,502-iteration epoch. Reviewed records show file edits 8–17 minutes after process exit and discrepancies with captured stdout. The case review notes that measured durations also satisfy the numerical intervals; the issue is reporting projections as measurements, not missing a target.

Authentic scores do not authenticate the accompanying record.

In Weak-and-Strong Verification, the case review finds genuine computed scores alongside edited audit records, including a FAIL-to-PASS change and backdated file timestamps. The case demonstrates why a valid numerical computation does not settle whether the submitted evidence faithfully represents the execution.

Appendix D Extended results and case evidence

D.1 Reference-variability strata

Both groups improve for every model, with larger gains in Cat. 1 for each model (Figure 8). Gains span 8.0 to 23.3 pp on stable tasks and 2.1 to 22.3 pp on higher-variability tasks. Wider compatibility intervals can accommodate larger numerical differences, and the task composition differs between strata; the contrast between groups is therefore descriptive.

D.2 Outcome transitions and execution diagnostics

An agent-assisted case review assigns primary explanations across 101 model–paper pairs (Table 16). Analysis agents inspect paired runs and refined-artifact documents; a consolidation agent reopens selected examples, and an independent reviewing agent challenges them. The categories describe explanations grounded in execution records. Their counts allocate the reviewed shares proportionally across recoveries; they are not independent causal measurements.

Protocol covers clarified settings and reporting rules; Launcher covers entry points and experiment-to-result mapping. Env covers compatible dependencies, and Code covers repairs or missing implementations. Artifact covers data/checkpoint acquisition and paths. Integrity concerns replacing measurement shortcuts with valid execution; audit-invalid names a scored outcome. Budget covers resource planning and scheduling; Other covers remaining explanations.

D.3 Failure modes and concentrated regressions

Failures shared by both handoffs.

Qualitative review of task–model pairs that fail with both raw code and refined artifacts identifies paper–code setup mismatches, typographical errors in the paper, and substantial experimental variability. A usable artifact can still preserve a setting that conflicts with the intended experiment or cannot resolve an erroneous paper statement. Even under a fixed procedure, a new observation can fall outside the reference compatibility interval.

Reversals after refinement.

A reversal is a task–model pair that succeeds with raw code but fails with the refined artifact; it differs from a net decrease over an entire paper. Table 17 partitions all 136 reversals by their refined-artifact outcome. Counts span four models, so a task can appear in several pairs. AuxiliaryMCMC contributes 50, Manifold-Aware Perturbations 19, LiME 14, and ExactFANOVA 10. These four papers account for 93/136 reversals (68.4%). A paper can contain both recovered and lost tasks: Gemini’s AuxiliaryMCMC total remains 12 successes in each condition despite five reversals offset by five recoveries.

AuxiliaryMCMC: numerical fragility interacts with a finite budget.

The Opus 5 refined-artifact Gaussian sweep for AuxiliaryMCMC (Yuan and Wang, 2026) targets 100 rounds at each of three acceptance rates. Its measured workload exceeds the available clock at the chosen concurrency, and the agent executes only 55 rounds per rate. The primary audit invalidates numerical matches affected by this altered measurement procedure. Separately, one Poisson-MALA chain remains constant with zero acceptance. Its undefined effective sample size propagates through the evaluator’s ordinary mean, leaving three measurements unavailable. The Reproducer declines to redraw only the failed chain, which would select a repetition based on its outcome. Effective sample size per second also varies with host load and concurrency.

The raw attempt also runs fewer than 100 rounds in part of its sweep. These records illustrate runtime constraints, numerical edge cases, and deviations from the prescribed measurement procedure.

LiME: setup success is not experiment completion.

In Sonnet 5’s refined-artifact attempt on LiME (Kowsher et al., 2026), data staging and environment preparation take approximately 83 minutes, but the full schedule includes 5,949 training steps followed by evaluation over 47 splits. The attempted run’s observed throughput projects 7 to 92 wall-clock hours per variant, competing within the paper’s 24-hour allocation. Model-construction parameter counts are available before training finishes, whereas accuracy measurements require completed training and evaluation. The session reaches the former but not the latter. Across models, 13 of LiME’s 14 reversals are resource/access failures and one is a numerical mismatch.

Interpreting residual numerical mismatches.

The 84 numerical reversals span several possible mechanisms: stochastic training, timing conditions, changed execution choices, and unresolved paper–code disagreements. Construction may also introduce an incorrect setting, metric interpretation, or repair that later agents inherit. Diagnosing a particular reversal requires tracing its executed configuration and measurement procedure. The Manifold-Aware Perturbations guide, for example, flags a learning-rate discrepancy between the paper and released code for further inspection (Appendix D.5).

D.4 Component ablations and reconstruction effort

We randomly select 12 papers from the 36-paper test set for the Sonnet 5 ablation. The same 287 tasks are evaluated across all seven conditions in Table 6; Table 18 lists the selected papers and their experiment and task counts.

For ordinary outputs, Opus 5 attempts reproduction with the raw codebase. Its execution directory, with result files removed but code, scripts, and logs retained, becomes the input codebase for a fresh Sonnet 5 session; no standardized documentation is added. This run and ReproBridge construction are separate upstream attempts with comparable resource use. ReproBridge receives the four-component delivery protocol from the start; the comparison evaluates the two workflows’ handoffs.

Section 4.5 defines the component removals and explains why descriptions of removed components are also deleted. The following case shows the reconstruction work that can return after removing the prepared environment.

WBMM without the prepared environment.

For WBMM (Song et al., 2026), the environment ablation retains experiment code and commands but removes the compatible H100 dependency route. Sonnet 5 reconstructs a Python 3.10 / PyTorch 2.0 / CUDA 11.8 stack with compatible vision libraries. A supplied binary lacks an operator’s H100 kernels, requiring a source rebuild before COCO evaluation. The agent also fixes an installation-tool compatibility issue and moves data off a quota-constrained shared filesystem. No paper-source patch is required, yet substantial environment work returns downstream. The trace produces measurements for all 58 selected tasks.

Timing measurements also depend on GPU concurrency and storage behavior. In this run, reuse of a smaller local image pool changes cache behavior alongside the reconstructed environment.

D.5 Worked reproduction examples

These examples expand the paired-run case evidence in Section 4.4, retaining exact configurations, task identifiers, and measurements. They illustrate information preserved in the refined artifact and corresponding recorded outcomes.

Recovering omitted configuration: HELIX.

For HELIX (Zhang et al., 2026a), Opus 5 restores the paper’s architecture on raw code but retains a shipped batch size of 32 and learning rate of approximately 6.29×10−46.29\times 10^{-4}. The guide’s ambiguity entry A6 identifies revision 9760b347, whose architecture matches the paper configuration, as the source for batch size 8 and learning rate 5.75×10−45.75\times 10^{-4}. The --paper_config launcher makes this choice executable. The recorded MAE changes from 0.15265 to 0.12986 for T004 and from 0.50527 to 0.41160 for T006; the respective compatibility intervals are [0.12524, 0.13448] and [0.38442, 0.43878]. The artifact records the repository history and architectural match as the rationale for adopting these settings.

An environment route that transfers: WBMM.

For six COCO tasks (T063–T068) in WBMM (Song et al., 2026), Sonnet 4.6’s raw attempt fails to install a compatible mmcv-full stack for H100. The refined artifact specifies matching PyTorch/MMDetection dependencies, the Ninja build prerequisite, and a source build for the target architecture. The downstream refined-artifact session makes no code patch and executes all six tasks. Its two box AP values, 51.61 and 52.78, agree numerically with reported targets 51.6 and 52.8; mask AP is 44.78/45.64 against 44.8/45.6. The artifact preserves an executable dependency route for later reuse.

Fixing validation labels: Effective Model Pruning.

The released TinyImageNet loader uses ImageFolder on a validation directory containing only an images subdirectory. It therefore assigns all 10,000 validation images to one class. During construction, ReproBridge adds a preparation script that places images into class directories using val_annotations.txt, verifies 200 classes and 10,000 images, and writes a preparation receipt required by the launcher. In Gemini 3.8 Flash’s paired runs, the ResNet-18 validation loss is 8.898 with raw code and 2.288 with the refined artifact, against the paper’s 2.303. This records a concrete repair and its downstream reuse.

Organizing measurement code for reuse: ETTFS.

The raw Opus 5 attempt searches the released ETTFS (Che et al., 2026) source for the metrics in Tables 2 and 3, finds no producing implementation, and leaves the inference-time measurement unexecuted. During construction, ReproBridge adds Code/profile_ttfs.py, documents the metric definitions and output fields, and supplies a launcher that trains a checkpoint before profiling it. The later Opus 5 session uses this explicit route and reports 2.0652 inference time steps against the paper’s 2.03. The artifact localizes code and resolved decisions that would otherwise require renewed investigation.

A measurement is not just a model execution: Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts.

For four-expert settings in Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts (De Santis et al., 2026), the paper does not specify how multiple expression distances should be reduced, and the repository provides no Table 1 collector. The raw Sonnet 5 attempt constructs a matching between learned and reference expressions but reports the sum of tree-edit distances. For two tasks this produces 60 and 188, whereas the per-expression means are 15 and 47. The refined artifact resolves the ambiguity by documenting the denominator and implementing the corresponding collector; those downstream values are 15 and 47. The case locates the discrepancy in the underspecified reporting statistic.

Preserving the experimental aggregation: SCIQL.

The released SCIQL (Petitbois et al., 2026) code produces run outputs but does not assemble the Table 1 statistic, leaving the mapping from logged fields and experiment settings to reported values incomplete. The raw Sonnet 4.6 attempt uses one default criterion, one seed, and an incorrect output column for a table statistic that averages across six criteria and five seeds. The refined artifact’s launcher and collector make this mapping explicit by specifying the sweep and the correct alignment field. One representative measurement changes from 19.70 to 55.66 against a paper value of 58.6. Criterion selection, output mapping, and repetition change together in this case, illustrating preservation of the complete measurement protocol.

An optimizer release is not a complete experiment: FlashOptim.

FlashOptim (Gonzalez Ortiz et al., 2026) supplies optimizer code but not the GPT-2 training and evaluation harness for the selected table. Gemini’s raw attempt leaves 18 GPT-2 outcomes unexecuted. The refined artifact adds a training/evaluation harness, data acquisition, output mapping, and launchers; all 18 pass in its recorded downstream attempt. The construction report lists 6,346 added lines of experiment support.

A localized repair: POET-X.

The defect occurs in examples/peft_pretraining/training_utils.py, line 222. Full batches call collate_fn, whereas the trailing partial batch is returned as a list. The evaluator calls batch.items(), so it fails when the final batch is reached. The patch changes the tail to yield collate_fn(batch). The record traces the sole caller to validation and describes CPU checks covering empty, partial, complete, and over-full batch counts, without changing the example count. This example illustrates how a later reproducer can recover both the fix and its experimental scope.

Flagging a setup discrepancy: Manifold-Aware Perturbations.

The guide’s ambiguity entry A1 contrasts the paper’s stated learning rate of 10−410^{-4} with the released driver, training scripts, and 171 committed manifests using 10−310^{-3}, and marks the discrepancy as high sensitivity. This gives authors a concrete inconsistency to inspect and resolve before submission.

D.6 Separate alignment analysis

A separate static audit compares selected paper results with their raw implementations. It distinguishes implemented behavior that contradicts the paper from absent implementations and details on which the paper is silent. Among 293 recorded findings, 238 are in scope for contradiction analysis and touch 669 distinct tasks. High-severity labels occur on 73 findings touching 482 tasks; 25 papers have at least one such finding. Task counts are deduplicated; a task may have multiple severity labels.

Agents produced these findings through static inspection of papers, code, and committed evidence. The analysis is separate from primary success scoring and covers the selected evaluation tasks. The evidence includes the learning-rate case above and a diffusion-objective case in which the code squares a norm described as an unsquared distance, changing its gradient. These cases illustrate that numerical compatibility and code execution can coexist with a paper–implementation discrepancy.

From an apparent gap to a localized finding.

The audit first extracts the paper-side requirement independently of the code-side inspection. It then identifies the implementation in that role, such as the function computing the loss or selecting the evaluation population. A contradiction requires an explicit paper statement and conflicting implemented behavior, with source locations and affected task IDs. If no implementation occupies the role, the finding is a missing implementation; if the paper specifies no relevant choice, it is underspecification rather than a contradiction. This separates 44 absent-implementation records and 11 paper-silent records from the 238 in-scope findings.

What these discrepancies mean.

A learning-rate disagreement is concrete even without retraining: one can point to the paper’s 10−410^{-4} and the code’s 10−310^{-3}. But the resulting change in final accuracy cannot be inferred from that factor alone. Similarly, replacing a distance by its square changes the objective and gradient weighting; its empirical impact requires a controlled comparison. The workflow records the contradiction and its scope while following the paper’s specified setup. These records can guide authors’ reproducibility checks before submission. In the terms of Section 2.1, the discrepancies are possible sources of DD, not estimates of its magnitude.

Severity is also an agent judgment. The record set assigns 73 findings a high label, of which 63 use an argued magnitude-based route and 10 concern inability to instantiate the stated setup. These labels help prioritize inspection. The alignment records were not supplied to the evaluated Reproducers.

D.7 Development-set results

We use Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash as Reproducers on the ten development papers: five from NeurIPS 2026 and five from ICLR 2026. Table 20 reports a single evaluation of reproduction success and downstream API spending under the same scoring definition as the test set. These papers informed workflow development, and their results are kept separate from the test-set aggregates.

Appendix E Cost accounting

Table 21 reports three-evaluation mean Reproducer costs, summing paper sessions within each evaluation. Claude tokens comprise input, output (including thinking), cache writes, and cache reads. Gemini totals include its separately recorded thinking field. The fixed per-million-token accounting rates, ordered as input/output/cache-write/cache-read, are (3,15,3.75,0.30)(3,15,3.75,0.30) for Sonnet 4.6, (2,10,2.50,0.20)(2,10,2.50,0.20) for Sonnet 5, and (5,25,6.25,0.50)(5,25,6.25,0.50) for Opus 5. Gemini rates are $0.75 for input, $3.75 for output plus thinking, and $0.075 for cache reads; recorded cache writes are zero.

Paper-session costs cover failed attempts and work beyond the 1,029 retained scoring tasks.

E.1 Construction investment and reuse

Constructing the 36 artifacts costs $5,026 in API usage, averaging $139.61 per paper.

Sources of construction effort.

The workflow provides a qualitative explanation of API expenditure. Specification requires reading the paper and code to resolve experiment settings and measurement rules. Execution support requires environment repair, missing implementation, and diagnosis through successive runs; each revision can require further code and log inspection. Review and packaging then check the evidence and preserve the resulting procedures. The WBMM dependency route and HELIX configuration recovery in Section 4.4, together with the FlashOptim training/evaluation harness in Appendix D.5, illustrate these kinds of work. GPU runtime is a separate expense: it affects API spending through associated model calls for setup, inspection, and debugging, not through elapsed GPU time itself.

Model-specific reuse.

For downstream model mm in {Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5}, let cmrawc_{m}^{\mathrm{raw}} and cmrefinedc_{m}^{\mathrm{refined}} be the mean paired aggregate API costs in Table 3, and let Cbuild=$5,026C_{\mathrm{build}}=\$5{,}026 be the full construction expense. One reuse round repeats the 36-paper workload represented by those costs. With stationary per-round spending, raw reuse costs n​cmrawnc_{m}^{\mathrm{raw}}, while refined-artifact reuse costs Cbuild+n​cmrefinedC_{\mathrm{build}}+nc_{m}^{\mathrm{refined}}. The API break-even count is

nm∗=⌈Cbuildcmraw−cmrefined⌉when ​cmraw>cmrefined.n_{m}^{*}=\left\lceil\frac{C_{\mathrm{build}}}{c_{m}^{\mathrm{raw}}-c_{m}^{\mathrm{refined}}}\right\rceil\quad\text{when }c_{m}^{\mathrm{raw}}>c_{m}^{\mathrm{refined}}.

Each model-specific scenario bears the full construction cost. For positive construction cost and nonpositive savings, there is no finite API crossover.

For example, Sonnet 5 costs a mean of $1,726 per raw round and $1,317 per refined-artifact round. The difference is $409; $5,026 divided by this saving is 12.29 rounds, hence 13 complete rounds to break even. The corresponding continuous crossover points are 7.70 rounds for Sonnet 4.6 and 8.17 for Opus 5, giving the 8 and 9 complete rounds reported in Section 4.7.

These scenarios repeat the complete 36-paper workload at fixed prices, caching, artifact contents, and agent behavior. Costs and savings are aggregated over paper sessions, including shared executions that produce multiple task scores. The crossover accounts for construction and downstream Reproducer API spending; independent auditing, GPU execution, maintenance, and unrecorded cache-storage fees are excluded. Human reference collection is a separate benchmark-development cost.
